extracted.intended_audience: novelists, students of fiction, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for constructing and evaluating novels, with emphasis on plot, character interplay, mystery/dénouement, and the use of fantasy/prophecy. Draws on examples (Meredith, Hardy, Gide, etc.) to illustrate effective and faulty techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot ought to cause surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: This shock, followed by the feeling, 'Oh, that's all right,' is a sign that all is well with the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good plot produces an unexpected incident that still feels acceptable once revealed. Example: the horse-whipping of Dr. Shrapnel in Beauchamp's Career is a surprising incident that reacts upon the book's world and transforms characters. Anti-pattern: predictable or purely mechanical incidents that produce no emotional or cognitive 'Oh, that's all right' resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incident must spring from character and alter character
rubrics_metrics.description: Incident springs out of character, and having occurred it alters that character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot events should arise plausibly from characters' natures and then affect those characters (cause-and-effect rooted in personality). Scoring note: incidents that feel grafted-on or arbitrary weaken the realism of characters. Meredith's method: people and events are closely connected because incidents are motivated by character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrivances are legitimate if they originate in character
rubrics_metrics.description: A Meredithian plot is not a temple ... but rather resembles a series of kiosks most artfully placed ... Incident springs out of character ... They are often delightful, sometimes touching, always unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrivances (artful devices, doors through which the book passes) when they flow from characters and affect them. Example: Meredith's contrivances transform personages without breaking verisimilitude. Anti-pattern: contrivances that feel arbitrary and do not react upon character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding inner life can serve plot but risks character integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Meredith has concealed the change. It would have spoiled his high comedy if we had been kept in touch with it throughout ... Charlotte Bronté's slip: she allows Lucy Snowe to conceal from the reader her discovery ... too much at the expense of Lucy’s character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concealing a character's inner development can create a dramatic thrill, but it may damage the reader's trust or the character's integrity if it contradicts the narrator's implied obligations. Use withholding deliberately and be mindful of narrator-character contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making plot dominate and sterilize characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The fate above us, not the fate working through us ... the characters have been required to contribute too much to the plot; except in their rustic humours, their vitality has been impoverished, they have gone dry and thin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware over-emphasis on causality or destiny that forces characters into mechanical roles. Example: Hardy's novels often order characters to acquiesce to plot, which diminishes their vitality (except Tess). Scoring note: assess whether characters retain individuality and vitality vs functioning solely as plot instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery and delayed revelation are essential to plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot requires mystery, but the mysteries are solved later on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining unanswered questions or concealed facts that are later revealed sustains reader interest. Use mystery to structure revelation; avoid premature exposition. Example formula cited: 'The queen died, it was afterwards discovered through grief.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing Aristotelian symmetry onto the novel
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an attempt to elevate the plot to Aristotelian symmetry, to turn the novel into a temple wherein dwells interpretation and peace. Meredith fails here: Beauchamp's Career remains a series of contrivances ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not impose rigid dramatic symmetry or moral neatness when it impoverishes the novel's character-driven complexity. Anti-pattern: shoehorning events to achieve tidy catharsis at the expense of the book's organic shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endings should not be mere mechanical winding-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all novels are feeble at the end. This is because the plot requires to be wound up ... the characters go dead while he is at work ... Death and marriage are almost his only connection between his characters and his plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid standard, bookish dénouements (relying solely on death or marriage) that kill characters' vitality. Strive for endings that preserve character life or that emerge organically rather than as logistical wrap-ups. Assess whether the dénouement feels inevitable and alive or forced and deadening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question planning vs organic growth of the novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Why has a novel to be planned? Cannot it grow? ... Instead of standing above his work and controlling it, cannot the novelist throw himself into it and be carried along to some goal that he does not foresee?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider allowing a novel to develop organically rather than strictly preplanning every detail. Gide's Les Faux Monnayeurs is invoked as an example where fragments, diaries, and emergent material coexist. Anti-pattern: over-planning that smothers spontaneity; conversely, lack of any shape may bore readers—balance is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fetishize plot as purely dramatic inheritance from the stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot is exciting and may be beautiful, yet is it not a fetich, borrowed from the drama, from the spatial limitations of the stage?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the novel can devise frameworks different from the play's tightly logical plot; invent novel-specific structures (fragments, diaries, meta-discussion) that suit fiction's capabilities. Gide's book demonstrates combining logical fragments with other methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy demands an extra contractual acceptance from the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy asks us to pay something extra. It compels us to an adjustment that is different ... The fantasist 'Here is something that could not occur. I must ask you first to accept my book as a whole, and secondly to accept certain things in my book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using fantasy, secure reader buy-in by establishing the book's terms; be aware some readers will refuse the additional 'sixpence'. Example: those who cannot accept the supernatural in Lady into Fox feel dissatisfied. Design the text so the required adjustment is earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy may require acceptance of the supernatural or its deliberate absence
rubrics_metrics.description: They ask us to accept either the supernatural or its absence. A thousand incidents suggest that it is not far off ... There is a charmed stagnation about the whole epic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the fantastic elements will be explicit or only intimated; both approaches can work. Maintain internal consistency: whether you include apparitions or only the suggestion of them, ensure their role is coherent with the book's atmosphere (e.g., Tristram Shandy's implied 'Muddle').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fantasy from prophecy by the scale and kind of mythology invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: They are alike in having gods, and unlike in the gods they have ... fantasy invokes Fauns, Dryads, little gods; prophecy invokes transcendent deities (India, Greece, Judea, Lucifer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an appropriate mythic register: the smaller, mischievous gods suit fantasy's tilts and improvisations; grand, transcendent deities suit prophetic, visionary fiction. Tone and device should match the scale of myth you invoke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fantasy devices knowingly—limited repertoire but fresh application
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices which writers of a fantastic turn have used—such as the introduction of a god, ghost, angel, monkey, monster, midget, witch into ordinary life; or the introduction of ordinary men into no man's land, the future, the past, the interior of the earth, the fourth dimension; or divings into and dividings of personality; or finally the device of parody or adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventory of fantastical devices is finite but endlessly reusable; select devices that fit temperament and aim, and try to put them to fresh use. Example: Flecker's Magic uses a wishing ring and witch-figure to explore modern desire; beware clichés and ensure the device serves character and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve fantasy's 'improvised air' while respecting core laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of fantasy penetrates into every corner of the universe, but not into the forces that govern it—the stars that are the brain of heaven, the army of unalterable law, remain untouched—and novels of this type have an improvised air, which is the secret of their force and charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a sense of spontaneity and playful tilt in fantastic fiction, but keep certain immutable rules intact so the fantastic feels intentional, not chaotic. Balance whimsy with limits; the beam-of-light image suggests a localized illumination that intersects but does not annihilate ordinary laws.
